title: Fostering students’ creative thinking through inquiry-design-based STEM water purification project
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether adding an explicit engineering design cycle to inquiry-based STEM learning improves secondary students’ creative thinking. The authors focus on a sustainability problem—designing a low-cost water purification system—and ask whether an Inquiry-Design-Based Learning integrated STEM model (IDBL-STEM) produces stronger gains than traditional inquiry-based learning (IBL) alone across four creativity dimensions: fluency, flexibility, originality, and elaboration.

The study was conducted with 10th-grade students in a public senior high school in Padang, West Sumatra, Indonesia. Two intact classes participated in a non-equivalent pretest-posttest control group design: one class received the IDBL-STEM intervention and the other received conventional inquiry instruction. The intervention lasted five sessions over three weeks and included problem exploration, investigation, prototype development, testing, and reflection. Students designed and built water purifier prototypes using recycled and locally available materials, and they also used AI-assisted image generation tools such as Microsoft Copilot, ChatGPT, or Google Gemini to visualize design ideas.

Results from ANCOVA showed that the IDBL-STEM group improved significantly more than the control group in fluency, flexibility, and originality, but not in elaboration. The authors conclude that iterative design embedded within inquiry is a strong mechanism for fostering divergent creative thinking in STEM classrooms, especially when learning is grounded in authentic environmental problems. They also note that elaboration may require more time and scaffolding, and they position the approach as relevant for sustainability education and the SDGs.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a quasi-experimental non-equivalent pretest-posttest control group study with ANCOVA and baseline equivalence checks, which supports moderate credibility. It is not randomized, so selection bias remains a concern, but the design and reporting are substantially stronger than purely descriptive work.
impact_tier_rationale: The study reports large effects for fluency and flexibility and a medium-to-large effect for originality (partial η²=.140-.262), indicating meaningful impact. However, the outcome is creativity rather than direct mathematics achievement, so the impact is strong on the measured construct but only indirectly relevant to the retrieval topic.

interventions.use_case: Inquiry-Design-Based Learning integrated with a STEM water purification project, where students iteratively designed, prototyped, tested, and refined low-cost water filters using recycled/local materials; AI image generation tools (e.g., Copilot, ChatGPT, Gemini) were used only as a support for visualizing designs, not as the main intervention.

AI-assisted image generation/visualization support for student design sketches during the water purifier project, including use of tools named ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, or Google Gemini to digitally visualize prototype concepts.

finding.finding_summary: The IDBL-STEM group showed significantly greater gains than the traditional IBL group in three creative-thinking dimensions: fluency, flexibility, and originality, but not elaboration. For fluency, the ANCOVA group effect was significant (F=25.17, p<.001, partial η²=.262) with n=72; for flexibility, F=22.84, p<.001, partial η²=.248; and for originality, F=11.23, p=.001, partial η²=.140. These outcomes were measured with a 10-item creative thinking scale using pretest-posttest scores, indicating stronger divergent thinking under the iterative design condition.
finding.measure: Creative thinking test scores and observational evidence for fluency, flexibility, originality, and elaboration

finding.finding_summary: The intervention was delivered in a science/biology context around environmental change and water purification, and students used scientific investigation, testing, and redesign to build and evaluate filtration prototypes. The paper reports that the IDBL-STEM condition improved students’ ability to connect scientific concepts with evidence-based testing and iterative refinement, although the primary measured outcome remained creative thinking rather than a direct science achievement test.
finding.measure: Prototype testing, data analysis during filtration trials, and science-based design performance documented through classroom observation
